$comment: AUTHORITY for the timing a Semiont client keeps: its deadlines, its retry budgets and the cadence of its stream. Every SDK generates its constants from this file, so one client waits as long, and tries as often, as another. A name ending in `Ms` is a duration in milliseconds; one ending in `Retry` is a budget of `attempts` with a backoff that starts at `initialDelayMs` and doubles to `maxDelayMs`; one ending in `Count` is a whole number of things. TypeScript: scripts/spec/generate-client-timing.mjs writes packages/typescript/core/src/generated/client-timing.ts. An SDK's testing surface may override any of these; these are what it does unasked. Which failures are worth an attempt is specs/src/retry/cases.json.

timing.name: busRequestTimeoutMs
timing.docs: How long a bus request waits for its reply. The gateway keeps a reply for redelivery at least twice this long (`replyRetentionSeconds` on POST /bus/subscribe), so a reply published during an outage is still there when the requester reconnects inside its own deadline.

timing.name: emitTimeoutMs
timing.docs: The deadline on one POST /bus/emit. The gateway accepts an emit promptly; one still unanswered here means the gateway is unresponsive, and the emit is rejected rather than awaited forever. Without it a worker's emit to a wedged gateway hangs its loop.

timing.name: emitRetry
timing.docs: The retry budget of ONE emit. Per request, never per boot pass: re-running a whole catch-up pass to recover from one refusal re-sends hundreds of emits that already succeeded. Small on purpose: an emit a caller awaits must fail while the caller still cares, and the patience for a gateway that is down belongs to the pass above it.

timing.name: httpRequestTimeoutMs
timing.docs: The deadline on one HTTP request that is neither the stream nor an emit: one of the gateway's own operations (who a token is, a media token, the resource metadata, health, status), the wait for a resource's bytes to begin arriving, a read of a resource's description or of its anchored text, a request to the issuer (its discovery, a grant, a revocation), and a read of a launcher's discovery document. Unanswered here, the request fails as one that got no answer. It bounds the read of a refusal's body too, of such a request or of the request that opens the stream (`streamOpenTimeoutMs`): a body not read by then is the refusal with none of the gateway's words, refused, renewed or retried as any refusal is. Without it, a gateway or an issuer that accepts a connection and never answers holds a session's start, and every renewal after it, for as long as the process lives. An upload has no deadline: how long it takes is how large the resource is. A read of anchored text may be held by the Archivist while the Smelter reads the content, for the time docs/protocol/ARCHIVIST.md states, and this deadline is longer than that wait.

timing.name: requestRetryPauseMs
timing.docs: The wait before an HTTP request that is neither the stream nor an emit is made a second time. It is made again when the gateway answered it with a status that promises recovery, or did not answer at all, on a method that cannot cause a second effect (`transport` in specs/src/retry/cases.json); once, after this wait, or after a refusal's `Retry-After` when that is longer. A request whose credential was refused is renewed and sent again at once, without this wait, and one unanswered at its deadline (`httpRequestTimeoutMs`) is not made again.

timing.name: streamOpenTimeoutMs
timing.docs: How long a client waits for the gateway to answer the request that opens its stream (POST /bus/subscribe): for the answer's status and headers. Unanswered here, the open has failed, and the stream is opened again on the backoff (`reconnectMs`), as after any open that failed. Without it, a gateway that accepts the connection and says nothing is waited on for as long as the process lives, and the stream is never opened again. The gateway answers an open as promptly as one of its own operations, so this is as long as `httpRequestTimeoutMs`. Only the answer is bounded here. An answer that refuses the open has its body read within `httpRequestTimeoutMs`, as any refusal's is: one not read by then is the refusal with none of the gateway's words. An open stream that carries nothing for a while has not failed, since a knowledge base where nothing happens has nothing to send.

timing.name: reconnectMs
timing.docs: The first wait before a failed stream is opened again. Each further failure doubles it, up to `maxReconnectMs`, and a successful open resets it. Also the cadence at which a transport with no usable credential checks for one, which costs no request.

timing.name: maxReconnectMs
timing.docs: The ceiling of the reconnect backoff: a long outage settles at about one attempt a minute instead of growing without bound.

timing.name: degradedThresholdMs
timing.docs: How long a stream may be reconnecting before its state becomes degraded.

timing.name: lingerMs
timing.docs: How long a superseded connection keeps draining after a make-before-break handoff. Closing it the instant its replacement opens discards replies already written to the old socket and not yet read. The overlap doubles nothing: a frame both connections carry has one id, and is delivered once (`seenEventIdsCount`).

timing.name: seenEventIdsCount
timing.docs: How many of the event ids it delivered last a client remembers. A frame whose id is among them is one it has delivered already, and is dropped: that is what makes a frame carried by both streams of a handoff, or replayed to the new one, arrive once. A client that remembers fewer delivers twice whenever more than that many events pass between the two copies.

timing.name: reconnectDebounceMs
timing.docs: How long additions to the subscription are gathered before the stream is reopened with them. Short, because a new scope needs to be live now.

timing.name: lazyRemoveMs
timing.docs: How long a removal from the subscription waits before the stream is reopened without it. Removal only narrows delivery, and reopening on every scope a viewer brushes past would churn the connection.

timing.name: refreshRetry
timing.docs: The retry budget of one token renewal: long enough to ride out a gateway restart or a rolling deploy, short enough that a user with no connectivity is told within seconds rather than a minute.

timing.name: refreshBeforeExpMs
timing.docs: The LARGEST margin before expiry at which a token is proactively renewed. A ceiling, not the margin: the margin is half the token's own lifetime, capped here. A fixed margin can equal the lifetime an issuer mints (Keycloak's default is five minutes), which makes every renewal already due: an idle signed-in page then sends over a hundred token requests a second.

timing.name: minRefreshDelayMs
timing.docs: The shortest the proactive renewal ever waits. A timer due now that reschedules itself on arrival is a closed loop; a floor makes that impossible, so even an issuer minting expired tokens gets one attempt per interval. Waiting is cheap here: a 401 still drives a renewal.

timing.name: devicePollMs
timing.docs: How long a sign-in by the device grant (RFC 8628) waits before each time it asks the token endpoint whether the person has approved the code, when the issuer's answer states no `interval`. RFC 8628 §3.2 names five seconds: an issuer that wants a client to ask less often says so.

timing.name: deviceSlowDownMs
timing.docs: How much longer a sign-in by the device grant waits between its asks, for that ask and every one after it, each time the issuer answers `slow_down`. RFC 8628 §3.5 names five seconds, so an issuer that says it again is given more time again.

timing.name: devicePollFloorMs
timing.docs: The shortest a sign-in by the device grant ever waits between its asks of the token endpoint, whatever `interval` the issuer states. An issuer that states zero, or a fraction of a second, would otherwise be asked again at once for as long as the code lives; a floor makes that impossible, as `minRefreshDelayMs` does for renewals. RFC 8628 sets no lower bound, and a second is not long enough for a person who has approved the code to notice.

timing.name: invalidationWindowMs
timing.docs: How long bus-driven invalidations of one cache key fold together (CACHE-SEMANTICS B19). The first runs at once; any more inside the window become one refetch at its end. Each refetch is a request the session's principal pays for, and another principal's bulk write invalidates an observed key once per event.

timing.name: saveDebounceMs
timing.docs: How long a cache that keeps its values waits, after they last changed, before it saves them (CACHE-SEMANTICS B17): a burst of changes is one save. Disposing the cache makes a save it owes at once.

timing.name: maxStoredBytesCount
timing.docs: The largest document, in bytes, a cache keeps of its values (CACHE-SEMANTICS B17). One larger loses the entries that have gone longest without a new value until it fits: what an origin may keep is a few megabytes, and the cache shares it with everything else the origin keeps.

timing.name: jobSilenceMs
timing.docs: How long a job a client is following may say nothing before the client asks for its status. A job's progress and its end reach the client as passing frames, which a dropped stream loses and nothing redelivers; `job:status-requested` is how a follower learns what it missed. Every frame of the job starts the wait again.

timing.name: jobStatusPollMs
timing.docs: How often a client asks for the status of a job that has been silent for `jobSilenceMs`, until the job says something or its status is an end.

timing.name: generationStallFloorMs
timing.docs: The shortest a client waits, with a generation it follows saying nothing, before it asks for the job to be cancelled and gives up on it. A floor, so a job that never says anything at all is caught whatever its size.

timing.name: generationStallPerTokenMs
timing.docs: How long a followed generation may be silent for each token it was asked for. A generation says nothing while its model writes, so the wait grows with the length of what was asked: four thousand tokens allow five minutes. The floor applies below it.

timing.name: generationStallAssumedTokensCount
timing.docs: The length assumed of a generation whose request states no `maxTokens`: the worker's own ceiling for one. At this length the floor decides the wait.

timing.name: delegateSilenceMs
timing.docs: How long a delegated job a client's state is following may say nothing before that state says the job has gone quiet (`mark:delegate-timeout`). Not a deadline on the job: the job goes on, the state keeps following it, and a completion that arrives later still ends it. Above the worker's heartbeat, so reaching it means silence and not a long call.

timing.name: jobClaimTimeoutMs
timing.docs: How long a party that takes jobs waits for the answer to one claim (`job:claim`). A claim is answered at once, with a job or with nothing pending; one still unanswered here is given up and reported as a refusal, and the party asks again at its next idle moment.

timing.name: heldJobStallMs
timing.docs: How long a held job may show no activity (its claim, a progress report, its settle) before whoever holds it calls it stalled. Not a limit on how long a job runs: one that keeps reporting is never stalled. The dispatcher's own sweep of running jobs is the backstop for a holder too wedged to notice.

timing.name: heldJobStallCheckMs
timing.docs: How often a party that holds a job looks at how long it has shown no activity.

timing.name: markCommitTimeoutMs
timing.docs: How long a worker waits for the record to acknowledge a commit of annotations (`mark:commit`), and then, when no acknowledgement came, for the answer to its question whether the batch's last annotation is on the resource (`browse:annotation-requested`). Generous beside an append, since a batch is a unit's annotations and the record may be catching up, and finite, since a wait on an acknowledgement that never comes would hold the job forever.

timing.name: generatedTextAsksCount
timing.docs: How many times a worker asks for the anchored text of a PDF it has just yielded (`GET /resources/{id}/anchored-text`) before it gives up on anchoring that PDF's citations. The text is the Smelter's to derive and is not there the moment the resource is. Each ask is answered at once when the text is stored, and otherwise waits at the Archivist for the Smelter to say it has settled the content (`smelt:settled`) before it is answered that the text is not there yet. So the count bounds the whole wait, and a worker that reaches it completes the job with the resource and without the citations.

timing.name: anchoredTextReaskMs
timing.docs: How long a viewer waits before it asks again for a resource's anchored text (`GET /resources/{id}/anchored-text`), after an answer that the text is not there yet or an ask that got no answer. The Archivist holds an ask while the Smelter reads the content and answers as soon as it has, so this wait is only for the answers that come at once: a text that is not there and is not being read, and a failure. A viewer does not annotate a resource until it holds the resource's text.

timing.name: hoverDelayMs
timing.docs: How long a pointer rests on an annotation before the viewer says it is hovered. Shorter, and a pointer crossing the page hovers everything on its way.

timing.name: searchDebounceMs
timing.docs: How long a search waits after its query last changed before it asks. A query still being typed is not asked for letter by letter.

timing.name: discoveryIntervalMs
timing.docs: How often a launcher's discovery document is read again, unless a caller says otherwise. A launcher rewrites it on every change to its stack, so a list of the knowledge bases it manages is a few seconds behind at worst, and the document is not read without pause.
